# Mobile PWA feasibility and open issues

Status: **prototype; do not present the pure-LAN PWA flow as a working mobile release**.
Reviewed 2026-10-10 and updated 2026-10-11 after discussion of changing desktop IPs.
This is the decision record to read before resuming mobile work. It records observed behavior,
code-derived failure modes, unverified claims, and the next architecture choice. It is not a
claim that every issue has been reproduced on a physical phone.

The follow-up discussion about a native Android APK, phone controls, and a GitHub-hosted
build is recorded in [android-apk-readiness.md](android-apk-readiness.md). Read both records:
this PWA prototype already has a phone-width shell, but it has no Android APK project.

## Intended path and its actual dependencies

```text
phone browser / installed PWA
  ├─ downloads its shell from the app host
  ├─ reaches a signaling relay over WebSocket to exchange SDP/ICE
  └─ opens WebRTC DataChannel + Noise to a desktop gateway hub
       └─ hub synchronizes encrypted event-log data with other LAN nodes over Noise/TCP
```

The signaling relay forwards connection setup; the **desktop gateway hub is in the data path**
between a phone and other nodes. It handles encrypted events and needs to be online and reachable.
The phone does not independently join the existing UDP multicast/TCP LAN mesh. The current
WebRTC setup gathers host candidates only, with no STUN/TURN fallback
(`crates/mesh-talk-core/src/gateway/mod.rs`, `frontend/src/lib/webrtcClient.ts`). Thus common
signaling alone does not guarantee a data path across isolated Wi-Fi clients, subnets, or the
internet.

## Release-blocking problems

| Area | What the branch does / why it can fail | Required resolution |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Changing desktop IP | `src-tauri/src/lan_host.rs::join_url` puts the current LAN IP and relay port in the QR URL. `frontend/src/lib/browserBackend.ts` saves the relay URL in localStorage and retries it. DHCP, switching Wi-Fi, or moving between Ethernet and Wi-Fi can make both URLs stale. | Use a discovery or rendezvous mechanism keyed by stable **node identity**, resolve its current endpoint on every reconnect, and test an IP change without rescanning. |
| Incomplete IP fallback | The desktop also advertises a `.local` mDNS name, but the phone learns that relay URL only after successful mesh gossip. A first connection cannot bootstrap from learned relays. Browser JavaScript cannot browse arbitrary LAN mDNS services; Android `.local` hostname resolution and multicast availability vary. Even a previously learned URL is only a fallback, not a guarantee. | Do not describe gossip or `.local` as zero-configuration recovery. Test on target Android devices/networks, or use native Android service discovery or a stable rendezvous service. |
| Origin-coupled identity | Opening `http://new-IP:port` gives the browser a different origin, with a different IndexedDB keystore and event log. `pwaNode.ts::loadNode` creates a **random new identity** if the keystore is absent. Entering the same password does not recover the old identity. | Keep one stable app origin and provide explicit encrypted backup/device linking before relying on browser storage. |
| HTTP is not an installable PWA origin | `frontend/DEPLOY.md` recommends `http://LAN-IP` and claims service-worker offline use and Add to Home Screen. A LAN IP over HTTP is not a secure context. On 2026-10-10, Chromium exposed service workers and camera APIs at `http://localhost`, but neither at `http://192.168.3.8`. It may still load as a web page, but it does not meet the intended secure PWA behavior. | Use a trusted HTTPS origin for the app and compatible `wss://` signaling. Verify installation, service worker, storage, and QR scanning on real phones. |
| Certificate confusion | WebRTC data channels use DTLS certificates/fingerprints created for the peer connection; they do not require a CA-issued website certificate. **Serving a PWA page** and its WebSocket signaling have separate HTTPS/WSS requirements. `ws://` from an HTTPS page is blocked as mixed content in the standard deployment. | Document and implement the browser-origin certificate and WSS plan. Do not ship an HTTP LAN page as a certificate-free PWA workaround. |
| Gateway start order | `set_relay_running` starts the native gateway hub only if `NodeRuntime` is already present. `spawn_node_runtime` later installs the runtime without starting a previously enabled hub. | Make gateway startup converge when both relay and signed-in node are ready; add a relay-before-login test and accurate health state. |
| Phone-first room | `browserBackend.ts::runMeshSync` treats the first browser participant as a hub/answerer; `gateway::run_mesh_hub` is always an answerer. If a phone enters first and the desktop joins later, both can wait for an offer. | Give the desktop a fixed authenticated gateway role or define deterministic role negotiation independent of join order; test both orders. |
| QR can point to a dead relay | `start_app_host` falls back to `PREFERRED_RELAY_PORT` in the URL when `relay_port` is absent. | Generate join links only after the relay and gateway are healthy and include the actual listening endpoint. |
| Misleading success | `browserBackend.ts::send_to_account` returns success when the recipient is unknown. `mesh-talk-wasm/src/lib.rs::sync_all_over_dc` discards individual `request_round` errors. | Surface send, per-conversation sync, and delivery states; do not show success for missing recipients or partial sync. |
| First-contact and session security | Signaling room join has no admission check (`mesh-talk-signal/src/lib.rs`). The browser initiates Noise with `expected_peer = None`; the QR carries a room/URL, not a trusted hub identity. `pwaNode.ts::saveSession` stores the password as plain JSON bytes in IndexedDB. | Authenticate pairing, bind the expected hub identity to it, pin that identity in the Noise handshake, and remove plaintext password persistence. |
| Foreground-only behavior | The sync loop runs in the page. The service worker caches the app shell; it does not maintain the WebRTC/Noise session or deliver messages while the page is suspended. | Specify foreground-only semantics, or choose a native mobile transport/background design if timely receipt is required. |

The branch also treats the PWA node as its own identity/account. It does not yet prove that a
phone can join the desktop user's existing multi-device account with the expected history and
device-link semantics. Decide this product behavior explicitly before calling it a mobile client.

## Evidence and gaps as of this review

- An isolated build of `origin/feature/mobile-pwa` passed frontend build, TypeScript checking,

- `pwa-gateway-sync.spec.ts` failed because the WebRTC data channel did not connect. A separate,
  minimal two-peer WebRTC test failed in the same Chromium environment and advertised a
  `198.18.0.1` virtual ICE candidate. This **does not prove a branch defect**; repeat on two
  physical devices on a normal LAN.
- `pwa-lan-bridge.spec.ts` is normally skipped unless release binaries and the E2E flag/CI are
  present. Its assertion is that the phone sees a second desktop in the roster; it does not
  assert phone → second desktop DM → reply. No physical Android end-to-end run was completed.
- The HTTP secure-context comparison above is a direct Chromium observation and agrees with
  current browser documentation.

## Architecture decision for the next discussion

**For a zero-setup, LAN-first Android experience, prefer a native Android APK using the shared
Rust core; Dioxus is one possible UI layer.** Use Android Network Service Discovery (DNS-SD/mDNS)
or the project's existing discovery through an Android-specific bridge to find the desktop's
current address, then use authenticated Mesh-Talk transport. Validate Android networking,
multicast permissions, Rust/Tokio integration, lifecycle, and packaging on devices; this is a
proposed direction, not an already proven implementation. The minimum proof is: install once,
discover desktop, exchange a DM with another desktop, change the gateway desktop's IP, then
rediscover and exchange another DM **without rescanning or re-pairing**.

If a PWA is still required, choose and prove one of these **stable bootstrap** designs first:

1. A stable HTTPS app origin and WSS rendezvous service. The desktop registers its current
   endpoint under a stable authenticated identity and re-registers after network changes; the
   phone reconnects and negotiates fresh ICE. Add TURN if isolated networks or remote access are
   in scope. This introduces service and internet dependencies.
2. A stable LAN DNS name with a trusted HTTPS certificate and WSS proxy, with a documented router
   or local-DNS setup and renewal procedure. A DNS-01 certificate can serve a private LAN name
   under a controlled public domain without exposing the LAN web port. This is workable for
   managed networks, not zero-setup on arbitrary Wi-Fi.

Do not use a DHCP reservation, current IP QR code, gossip-only fallback, or `.local` alone as a
general solution to dynamic addresses. Whatever approach is chosen must also show reconnect
state to the user and distinguish **queued**, **synced to gateway**, and **delivered to recipient**.

## Acceptance gates before a mobile release claim

1. Two real desktops plus Android phone: phone ↔ non-gateway desktop DM, both directions; verify
   message contents and delivery state, not only roster presence.
2. Repeat after gateway IP changes, relay restart, desktop login after relay startup, phone-first
   join, app restart, and stale endpoint cache; no rescan or silent identity reset.
3. Test ordinary Wi-Fi, guest/client-isolated Wi-Fi, different subnets, and screen-off/resume;
   state clearly which topologies and background behavior are supported.
4. Verify trusted origin, installability, service worker, QR camera, WSS, ICE, Noise peer pinning,
   unauthorized-room rejection, and storage recovery on target Android browsers if PWA remains.

### REQ-030 — Comprehensive code verification and a maintained testing/feedback system

- **Discussion state:** Clarifying; broad verification requirement and supplied reference taxonomy captured; applicability, tools, gates and implementation not selected.
- **Captured / updated:** 2026-11-17 (Asia/Singapore).
- **Original user request:** “调研的以后再做吧，先整理好需求相关信息就行了。第30个需求，使用以下测试手段对整个app，项目进行充分的测试，并建立健全的测试机制”。 User supplied a “Code Verification Atlas” covering the methods and dimensions below.
- **Scenario and affected users:** Whole-app/project quality across AI/developer iteration, review, release and recovery. The aim is sustained evidence of correct, secure, performant and reliable behavior, not only more test files.
- **Desired outcome:** A comprehensive, maintained verification strategy with appropriate complementary methods, meaningful assertions and actionable feedback across the project's risks and acceptance requirements.
- **Confirmed topic scope:** Consider the full supplied verification landscape for the whole app/project and establish a sound testing mechanism. Do not silently drop advanced methods; assess their fit and evidence value later. Named tools are examples from the reference, not selected dependencies or a requirement to run every tool on every change.

#### User-supplied verification landscape — retained for later assessment

| Family | Methods/dimensions supplied | Focus retained |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Static verification | Syntax, type and semantic checking; static analysis; SAST; formal verification | AST/scope/type validity, control/data flow, dead code/complexity, security findings and model/invariant reasoning |
| Dynamic verification | Unit, integration, E2E and contract tests | Local behavior, boundaries/dependencies, complete workflows and interface compatibility |
| Generative/test-effectiveness techniques | Property-based testing, fuzzing and mutation testing | General properties, malformed/adversarial input and whether tests detect meaningful code defects |
| Runtime and dynamic security | Runtime assertions/contracts/monitors and DAST | Executed invariants, running-interface security and failure behavior |
| Performance | Benchmarks, load, stress, spikes, soak/stability and capacity tests | Latency/throughput/resource budgets, growth and sustained workload behavior |
| Memory/concurrency | Memory safety/leaks, undefined behavior and data-race checking | Correct cleanup, memory/concurrency faults and supported instrumentation |
| Coverage | Statement, branch, condition, function, path and MC/DC coverage | Evidence of what was exercised; applicability/feasibility and assertion quality need separate assessment |
| Maintainability | Code review, complexity, duplication, code smells and technical debt | Change locality, understandable contracts and maintainable implementations |
| Security/SCA | Vulnerabilities/CVEs, secrets, dependency and supply-chain review | Code and dependency risks with actionable findings |
| Compliance | Licensing, coding rules, data protection and relevant standards | Determine actual obligations; cited MISRA/AUTOSAR are examples, not assumed Mesh Talk requirements |
| Reliability/resilience | Fault injection, tolerance, degradation, recovery and chaos tests | Failure/recovery correctness and supported fault assumptions |
| AI/ML and LLM/Agent evaluation | Data quality, behavior, fairness/robustness/regression; prompt/output structure; tool-call correctness; multi-turn completion; hallucination/factual consistency; safety/authorization; RAG retrieval/citations; end-to-end evals | Evaluate only actual modeled AI/agent surfaces and defined risks; do not add an LLM/RAG product solely to use these techniques |

**Example tools from supplied reference — unselected:** Compilers/parsers/IDEs; TypeScript/Rust/mypy; SonarQube/ESLint/Semgrep/CodeQL/Fortify; TLA+/Alloy/Dafny/Coq/Lean; JUnit/pytest/Jest/Go test/Testcontainers/Selenium/Cypress/Playwright/Pact; QuickCheck/Hypothesis/fast-check/AFL++/libFuzzer/OSS-Fuzz; PIT/Stryker/mutmut; runtime assertions; OWASP ZAP/Burp Suite; JMeter/k6/Gatling; ASan/LSan/UBSan/TSan/Valgrind; JaCoCo/Coverage.py/Istanbul/Checkstyle; Snyk/Trivy/Dependabot; Chaos Mesh/LitmusChaos; DeepEval/Ragas. **REQ-030 是「充分验证整个 Mesh Talk，并建立长期可维护的测试与反馈机制」。** 它要解决的是每次改动后，团队能知道哪些行为已经验证、失败在哪里，以及发布前还缺什么证据。

它涵盖三个层面：

- **验证功能和边界。** 用静态检查、单测、集成测试和端到端测试覆盖核心流程，包括权限、离线重连、数据恢复和升级。

- **把验证融入开发流程。** 日常开发能快速跑受影响的检查。PR 和发布阶段补齐跨平台、原生和完整场景的证据。报告应区分通过、失败、取消和待验证。

# Documentation guidelines

Mesh-Talk documentation should help a reader make a decision or complete a task.
Keep one coherent product story across surfaces, with details in the document that
owns them. A feature does not need a new paragraph everywhere it is mentioned.

## Audience and ownership

| Surface                                                      | Reader's question                                                     | Owns                                                                                                                                               |
| ------------------------------------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| [Project site](../site/index.html)                           | Is Mesh-Talk for me?                                                  | Product model, trust boundaries in plain language, representative UI, download and documentation paths.                                            |
| [Root README](../README.md)                                  | What is it, how do I start, and where is the source?                  | Concise orientation, supported communication paths, first run, repository map.                                                                     |
| [Documentation hub](README.md)                               | Which guide answers my question?                                      | Task-based routes and a complete catalog of maintained guides and evidence.                                                                        |
| [Architecture](ARCHITECTURE.md)                              | How does the system work?                                             | Protocol, modules, data flow, crypto, wire compatibility, and technical limits.                                                                    |
| [Network architecture baseline](network-design-reference.md) | Which communication model and contracts must future changes preserve? | Network design principles, module ownership, topology scenarios, policy interactions, resource budgets and feature-specific acceptance boundaries. |
| Feature and operations guides                                | How do I configure or use this capability?                            | Exact steps, options, examples, constraints, and troubleshooting for their topic.                                                                  |
| [Evaluation inputs](evals/README.md)                         | Which reusable cases and rubrics apply?                               | Maintained suites, inventory and prompts; generated evidence belongs in PR/CI artifacts.                                                           |

The site and README may summarize a capability, but link to its owning guide
for setup, flags, support matrices, and changing limits. Do not copy a CLI option
table, release procedure, or full feature inventory into either overview.

The [change alignment checklist](maintenance-checklist.md) owns the cross-surface
maintenance inventory: select applicable items when behavior changes, identify
generated and externally published consumers, and record evidence or follow-ups
in the PR. This guide owns writing and audience rules; the checklist links to
existing owners rather than duplicating their product contracts.

## Shared domain language

[CONTEXT.md](../CONTEXT.md) owns domain definitions; [DDD conventions](domain-design.md)
own modeling vocabulary, identifier mappings and the reference index. Use those
terms in guides, code comments and reviews. Keep technical invariants in the
architecture/network references and implementation ownership in the module map.
Do not create feature-local glossaries that redefine account/device identity,
conversation membership, lifecycle or delivery outcomes.

## Shared project narrative

Explain the whole communication model in this order, regardless of which feature
changed most recently:

1. **Encrypted communication on a LAN:** local identities, signed discovery and
   authenticated direct connections; no internet or central messaging service is

s=s[:i]+'''#### Search implementation and review

[SearchDialog](../frontend/src/features/chat/SearchDialog.tsx) calls
[owner-scoped IPC](../src-tauri/src/owner_commands/search.rs), which dispatches
blocking work through runtime admission to [core search](../crates/mesh-talk-core/src/node/search.rs).
The [history dialog](../frontend/src/features/chat/ConversationHistoryDialog.tsx)
has a separate per-conversation path. Its
[explicit remote-history paging](channel-history-paging-ui.md) does not expand
the global search query's coverage by itself.

Global search normalizes the query and compares case-folded substrings in the
existing history projection. It maintains no separate full-text index or
index rebuild job. The host rejects an overlong query before scheduling and
serializes a bounded newest-first result prefix. The UI discards an obsolete
response, but that discard does not cancel a core scan already admitted.

Keep canonical identities and visibility checks in the history owner. Before
changing the implementation, measure metadata traversal, body reads and query
latency with short and long retained histories and rapid query replacement.
If metadata traversal dominates, first test bounded history selection with
the same coverage and ordering. A separate full-text index would require
evidence of user need and tests for protected content, recall, expiry,
deletion, rebuild and write amplification.

'''+s[i:]
i=s.index('## 6. Binaries')
s=s[:i]+'''## Operational logging and diagnostic exports

The [desktop logger](../src-tauri/src/logger/mod.rs) is installed during
[Tauri setup](../src-tauri/src/lib.rs). Rust producers use the \`log\` facade.
The desktop writes local-time records to \`logs/mesh-talk.log\` under its
configured data root, normally \`~/.mesh-talk\`. Debug builds also write to
stdout. Debug builds admit Debug and higher by default, release builds Warn
and higher. Graphics, startup and selected core targets also admit Info.
The log stream is process-wide and can contain earlier session context.

The application uses the file defaults of \`tauri-plugin-log\` 2.10.2, pinned
in [Cargo.lock](../Cargo.lock). The plugin opens the active file in append
mode and rotates around its 40,000-byte threshold with \`KeepOne\`, replacing
the active file rather than preserving an archive at each rollover. The
application also attempts to delete \`.log\` files older than seven days during
logger initialization. This sweep is best effort and startup-driven. Seven
days therefore describes the cleanup cutoff, not available diagnostic history.

Diagnostics uses [typed commands](../frontend/src/lib/api/diagnostics.ts)
to read or export up to the last 64 KiB of the current file. The host seeks
and reads on a blocking worker. It returns an empty string if the active
file is absent and decodes lossily if the byte boundary splits a character.
[Diagnostics authority](../src-tauri/src/diagnostics.rs) checks the originating
session and lock state before publishing a read or admitting a save. Copy
and Save expose raw log text. Review it before sharing. See
[diagnostic exposure and authority](privacy-controls.md#reducing-address-and-identity-exposure).

With \`MESH_TALK_TRACE_WORK=1\`, the desktop also counts registered IPC dispatch
attempts by command name, with at most 256 names per window and a drop counter.
Handled requests drive emission after a five-second window. The observer
starts no periodic worker and records no arguments. The
[headless CLI](../crates/mesh-talk-core/src/bin/mesh-talk-node.rs) installs a
separate opt-in sink for selected SQL work records. It does not share the
desktop file sink. Operational logs and these counters serve diagnostics.
The [signed event log](#3-event-log--sync-eventlog) serves durable protocol
reconciliation, and the history projection serves chat views.

Retain bounded on-demand log export. Verify rollover and failure behavior on
packaged hosts before changing rotation, buffering or severity. If useful
startup context is consistently lost, measure rollover frequency and
idle writes before choosing a retention budget. If reports need sharing
without manual review, define and test a separate redacted export mode.

'''+s[i:];p.write_text(s)
PY

# labali-git-auto-commit-rewrite

## NEVER

- **Never fabricate diff content** or invent changes not present in `git diff` output — a fabricated commit message is worse than no message; it destroys trust in git history.
- **Never amend a previous commit** — always create a new commit. Amending rewrites history and can silently overwrite commits that others (or hooks) have already acted on.
- **Never use `--no-verify`** to bypass pre-commit hooks — the hooks are the project's safety net; bypassing them defeats their purpose and masks real issues.
- **Never write a body that only lists filenames** — `- update core.ts` tells nothing; name the intent behind the change, not the file that changed.

# Good Commit Message Examples

These examples demonstrate the target quality for commit messages generated by this skill.

---

## Example 1 — Feature with clear scope

```
feat(skill): add license and compatibility fields to all SKILL.md frontmatter
```

**Why it works:**
- Subject is specific and action-oriented, under 72 chars
- Body bullets map to real grouped changes, not generic "update files"
- Scope `(skill)` accurately signals the affected area

- add Quick Links table in AGENTS.md for per-task doc loading

---
name: research
description: Investigate a question against high-trust primary sources and capture the findings as a Markdown file in the repo. Use when the user wants a topic researched, docs or API facts gathered, or reading legwork delegated to a background agent.
---

Spin up a **background agent** to do the research, so you keep working while it reads.

Its job:

1. Investigate the question against **primary sources** — official docs, source code, specs, first-party APIs — not a secondary write-up of them. Follow every claim back to the source that owns it.
2. Write the findings to a single Markdown file, citing each claim's source.
3. Save it where the repo already keeps such notes; match the existing convention, and if there is none, put it somewhere sensible and say where.
### Storage replay and query budgets

The indexed-storage connection owner in `storage/database.rs` uses SQLCipher
for encrypted and authenticated database pages, including indexes and WAL data.
It verifies the application/schema version and encrypted owner binding before
use, and never replaces unreadable storage with an empty database. A profile
shares one serialized connection; domain stores own their tables and bounded
queries. SQLCipher passphrases are domain-separated so user input cannot select
the raw-key syntax. Production key derivation retains a 600,000-iteration
password work factor; only existing test configurations reduce it.

Opt-in transaction work diagnostics use `MESH_TALK_TRACE_WORK=1` and retain
at most 64 static caller locations per connection in a 30-second observation
window, with aggregate overflow counters. They record committed transaction and
changed-row counts, never SQL text, bound values, account identities or runtime
file paths. Observation uses nonblocking admission after the database guard is
released; logging also occurs after the observation guard is released. Disabled
owners retain no diagnostic collector. These logical work counts do not measure
physical disk bytes; native filesystem tracing owns that acceptance evidence.

The desktop IPC adapter uses the same opt-in flag for a separate metadata-only
observer: at most 256 registered command names of at most 96 ASCII bytes. It
counts handled dispatch attempts, excluding lock rejection and unhandled names,
never arguments, results or private state. Nonblocking admission reports dropped
counts; the next accepted invocation can emit a five-second summary after the
observer guard is released. There is no new timer or worker. Default mode creates
no collector, command-name allocation or diagnostic output; these counts establish
request frequency rather than successful execution or CPU cost.

Settled fixed-consumer reception retirement performs no SQL mutation when
its durable retirement cursor has not advanced. The same bounded transaction
still checks account/lifetime ownership and drains pending metadata: an ACK
committed before a cleanup failure must allow cleanup to resume after reopen
without requiring another ACK.

Device-local [reception source](network-design-reference.md#device-local-reception-source)
uses fixed-size metadata alongside newly admitted raw events. Its transactional
schema-only procedure. It preserves retained payload pages and foreign keys;
interruption rolls back the version and definition together. Unknown or weakened
schemas fail explicitly. Capability probes use a covering kind index and never
load retained bodies; a newly required v5 control invalidates an older sync view.

Fresh encrypted databases establish incremental auto-vacuum (mode 2) before the
first metadata table. Warm open authenticates application/schema and owner first,
then requires the same mode. Unsupported NONE/FULL modes fail without a full
VACUUM, initialization over existing authority or an empty-store fallback.
Authenticated legacy publication creates its new database with this policy.

Connection policy disables mmap, keeps temporary data in memory, suggests a
4 MiB page cache, and uses FULL synchronization with a 256-page automatic WAL
checkpoint trigger and a 4 MiB retained-journal target. A connection also retains
at most 64 prepared SQL statements. Relay inventory, session authority, maintenance,
canonical source/owner guards, projection reads and network metadata selectors
share this fixed cache; the former 16-entry bound
recompiled warm queries as these paths displaced each other. Reused statements
still execute every eligibility, readiness, expiry, revision, session and lifecycle
check against the current transaction. Query results are
not cached, and returned statements clear their bound values. These are connection budgets,
not a global RAM or disk cap: query results, concurrent domain work, long readers
and historical data require their own bounds. Failed commits, failed rollbacks
and fatal storage errors invalidate the handle until reopening. Read failures
remain errors rather than missing records. The connection owner does not by
itself convert legacy event or transcript stores to demand loading.

L316:   * Per-group wrappers - one `MetaGroupWrapperNode` instance per group, keyed by its `03`-prefix pubkey

L320: More details about this protocol can be found in the 【77†libsession-util-nodejs】 and the 【78†libsession-util】 repos.
L321: The `MetaGroup-{03pubkey}` wrapper is a special case for multiple reasons:
L322: 
L323:   * it is not a singleton, but a per-group wrapper
L324:   * it is not a 1to1 mapping to the libsession-util API, but a merged wrapper of the GroupInfo, GroupMembers, and GroupKeys configs. See 【79†libsession-util】

L326: * * *
L327: ## 5. State Management
L328: 
L329: Application state is managed with Redux Toolkit. The store is created in `ts/state/createStore.ts` and uses `redux-promise-middleware` for async action handling.
L330: ### Store Shape
L331: 
L332: The top-level reducer (`ts/state/reducer.ts`) composes the following slices:
L333: Slice  | Contents
L334: --- | ---
L335: `conversations`  | Conversation list per-conversation metadata & selected conversation messages
L336: `user`  | Own account (Session ID, display name, avatar)
L337: `search`  | Search query and results
L338: `settings`  | User-configurable preferences
L339: `theme & primaryColor`  | Active theme and colors
L340: `section`  | Global layout of the app
L341: `modals`  | Open modal dialogs and their props
L342: `call`  | Voice / video call state
L343: `onionPaths`  | Currently-active onion paths & online status
L344: `stagedAttachments`  | Attachments staged to an outgoing message
L345: `userGroups`  | Closed group and community list
L346: `metaGroups`  | Extended group metadata (derived from libsession)
L347: `networkData`  | Sesh details fetched from the server
L348: ### Patterns
L349: 
L350:   * Ducks layout - each slice lives in its own file under `ts/state/ducks/`.
L351:   * Reselect - memoised selectors live in `ts/state/selectors/` and are the only way components should derive computed values from state.
L352:   * Class vs Functional components - functional components are preferred over class components, but we still have some left in `ts/state/smart/`
L353: ### ConversationModel → Redux update flow
L354: 
L355: `ConversationModel` (`ts/models/conversation.ts`) does not use Backbone or a custom event emitter. When its attributes change, it pushes updates into Redux directly:
L356: 
L357:     `ConversationModel.set(attrs)
L358:       └─▶ triggerUIRefresh()
L359:             └─▶ getConversationModelProps()   // serialise to plain props object
L360:                   └─▶ dispatch(conversationsChanged([props]))
L361:     `
L362: Components usually don't hold a reference to a `ConversationModel`. They select plain data from the Redux `conversations` slice and re-render when the slice changes.
L363: 
L364: When many conversations change at once (e.g. during a bulk import or config sync), updates are batched through `throttledAllConversationsDispatch()` to avoid one Redux dispatch per message.
L365: `ConvoHub` (`ts/session/conversations/ConversationController.ts`) is the in-process registry. It is the only place that creates or looks up `ConversationModel` instances - call `ConvoHub.use().get(pubkey)` or `ConvoHub.use().getOrCreateAndWait(pubkey)` rather than constructing models directly.
L366: 
L367: * * *
L368: ## 6. Database Layer
L369: 
L370: ### Technology
L371: 
L372: All persistent data is stored in a single SQLCipher database. The database file lives in the Electron user-data directory. Because SQLCipher runs as a native addon, it can only be used in the main process.
L373: ### Access Pattern
L374: 
L375:     `Renderer ──(IPC)──▶ ts/node/sql_channel.ts ──▶ SQLCipher (main process)
L376:     `
L377: 
L378: The renderer never calls SQL directly. It calls typed wrappers in `ts/data/` which serialise & clean arguments and dispatch them over named IPC channels. Results are returned as plain JSON objects. This arrangement:
L379: 
L380:   1. Keeps the database in a single process, avoiding concurrent-write issues.
L381:   2. Enforces a clear API boundary between UI logic and persistence.
L382: ### Key Tables
L383: Table  | Contents
L384: --- | ---
L385: `conversations`  | Contact and group metadata
L386: `messages`  | Message content, type, status, timestamps
L387: `messages_fts`  | FTS5 full-text search index over message bodies
L388: `nodesForPubkey`  | cached swarm nodes for a given pubkey
L389: `identityKeys`  | User Ed25519 & x25519 key pairs
L390: `items`  | Key/value settings store
L391: `openGroupRoomsV2`  | Open community (SOGS) room metadata
L392: `seenMessages`  | hashes of processed messages (deduplication)
L393: `configDump`  | Serialised (hex) libsession config dumps
L394: ### In-Memory Models
L395: 
L396: `ConversationModel` and `MessageModel` (under `ts/models/`) wrap database rows with business logic and event emission. `ConvoHub` acts as an in-process registry that caches loaded conversation objects, lazily fetching from the database on app start.
L397: 
L398: * * *
L399: 
L400: ## 7. Networking and Messaging
L401: ### The Session Network
L402: 
L403: Session Desktop communicates with a decentralised network of service nodes. Each user's messages are stored on a swarm - a subset of nodes responsible for that user's Session ID. The app periodically polls its swarm for new messages and pushes outgoing messages to the recipient's swarm.
L404: 
L405: For groups, the group gets its own pubkey and so its own swarm. Every member of the group will periodically poll the group swarm in addition to its own swarm.
L406: All traffic is wrapped in onion routing: three service nodes are selected at random to form a path, and the request is layered in encryption so that no single node sees both the origin and the destination.
L407: 
L408:     `App ─▶ Guard Node ─▶ Middle Node ─▶ Exit Node ─▶ Destination
L409:             (knows src)               (knows dst)
L410:     `
L411: The path building logic is making sure that the nodes in the path are not in the same subnet. We also keep multiple paths in case one of them fails, or in case we need to store a message to a node that is already on our current path.
L412: ### Sending
L413: 
L414:     `ts/session/sending/
L415:     ├── MessageQueue.ts          # Priority queue; retries on failure
L416:     ├── PendingMessageCache.ts   # Tracks in-flight messages in the DB
L417:     ├── MessageSender.ts         # Encrypts and dispatches to service nodes
L418:     └── MessageWrapper.ts        # Protobuf serialisation + padding
L419:     `
L420: `MessageQueue` ensures messages are sent in order per conversation. Failed sends are retried with exponential back-off. The `PendingMessageCache` survives app restarts so no messages are silently lost.
L421: 
L422: Some calls don't need to be retried, or the retries are handled manually. For those, use the `sendToPubKeyNonDurably` method.
L423: ### Receiving
L424: 
L425: `ts/session/apis/snode_api/swarmPolling.ts` runs a background loop that polls each swarm the user is subscribed to. Fetched envelopes are passed to `ts/receiver/receiver.ts`, which:
L426: 
L427:   1. Verifies the sender signature.
L428:   2. Decrypts the envelope with the recipient's private key.
L429:   3. Dispatches the inner content message to the appropriate handler (`contentMessage.ts`, `dataMessage.ts`, etc.).
L430:   4. Writes the result to the database and updates Redux state.
L431: This whole process has to be fast so no network calls should be made while handling a message. For anything that needs to be done on the network while processing a message, a job should be added (if retries are needed) or the network call should be `void` so that it doesn't delay processing of other messages. For instance when we receive a message, we sometimes need to fetch a user's new profile picture from the file server.
L432: This is done by adding a new job that will fetch that file, but the fetch itself is not part of the message processing pipeline.
L433: ### Open Groups (SOGS)
L434: 
L435: Community rooms are served by Session Open Group Servers (SOGS), accessed via the `ts/session/apis/open_group_api/` client. Communities usually use blinded Session IDs so joining one does not expose your own SessionID . Blinded IDs start with `15` or `25`.
L436: ### Libsession Config Layer
L437: 
L438: The `libsession_util_nodejs` native addon manages config messages - a CRDT-based mechanism that synchronises user details, contact list, groups and current read state across multiple devices. Config operations are executed inside the `libsession.worker.ts` Web Worker to avoid blocking the UI thread. See 【80†§4 - libsession Worker Protocol】 for the wire format.
L439: ### insecureNodeFetch
L440: 
L441: `ts/session/utils/InsecureNodeFetch.ts` is a thin wrapper around `node-fetch`. The name is intentionally alarming - it should never gain new call sites without a clear justification.
L442: 
L443: It is acceptable in its current call sites for a few reasons:
L444:   1. Seed node requests - the certificate of those are pinned and embedded in the app (see `ts/session/apis/seed_node_api/SeedNodeAPI.ts`)
L445:   2. Guard node - these are already encrypted at the onion routing layer.
L446:   3. Public external calls (link previews, Giphy API) - these do not go through the onion logic and are leaking metadata. They are disabled by default and can only be enabled after a warning about their use is approved.
L447: The wrapper also serves as the online-state detector: if a request throws a network-unreachable error (`ENETUNREACH`, `EHOSTUNREACH`), it calls `setIsOnlineIfDifferent(false)` to flip the app's connectivity state. This is why virtually all outbound network requests funnel through it rather than calling `fetch` directly.
L448: Each call site tags its traffic with a `FetchDestination` enum value (`SERVICE_NODE`, `SEED_NODE`, `SOGS`, `PUBLIC`) for debug logging when the `debugInsecureNodeFetch` feature flag is enabled.
L449: ### Snode Pool and Swarm Selection
L450: 
L451: The app bootstraps its view of the network from a small hardcoded list of seed nodes. On first run (and periodically thereafter), it fetches the full snode pool (currently 1600+ nodes) from the seed or via a combination of snodes.
L452: 
L453: For each pubkey the user is subscribed to, `ts/session/apis/snode_api/getSwarmFor.ts` requests the responsible swarm from the pool and caches the result. Swarm membership is re-fetched lazily when the swarm of a pubkey is becoming too small.
L454: Guard node selection (`ts/session/onions/onionPath.ts`): 2-4 nodes are pinned as persistent entry points for onion paths. Those are the nodes we are exposing our IP too. As long as they are reachable, they shouldn't be changed. They are saved in a database table so they survive restarts. When building a path, subnet isolation is enforced - to limit the risk of a single ISP observing both the origin and an intermediate/exit node.
L455: Nodes that fail requests are dropped from the in-memory pool and logged. Paths that accumulate too many failures are torn down and rebuilt.
L456: ### Group Versions: Legacy (05-prefix) vs Groups v2 (03-prefix)
L457: 
L458: There are two incompatible closed-group implementations coexisting in the codebase:
L459:  | Legacy Closed Groups  | Groups v2
L460: --- | --- | ---
L461: Pubkey prefix  | `05` (Ed25519)  | `03` (Curve25519)
L462: Conversation type  | `ConversationTypeEnum.GROUP`  | `ConversationTypeEnum.GROUPV2`
L463: Config storage  | Legacy protocol  | `MetaGroupWrapper` via libsession worker
L464: Detection  | `isClosedGroup() && !isClosedGroupV2()`  | `isClosedGroupV2()`
L465: Disappearing msgs  | DaS only, control msgs never expire  | DaS forced; same control-msg rule
L466: Status  | Read only, cannot retrieve/send msgs  | Actively used, read/write possible
L467: The predicates `PubKey.is05Pubkey(id)` and `PubKey.is03Pubkey(id)` in `ts/session/types/PubKey.ts` are the canonical way to distinguish them. New feature work should target Groups v2 only as the legacy ones are readonly.
L468: 
L469: * * *
L470: ## 8. Snode Namespaces
L471: 
L472: Every message stored on or retrieved from a service node is placed in a namespace - a numeric partition of a swarm's storage. Namespaces separate message types so the app can poll, authenticate, and prioritise them independently. The full enum is defined in `ts/session/apis/snode_api/namespaces.ts`.
L473: ### Namespace Reference
L474: Namespace  | Constant  | Stores  | TTL
L475: --- | --- | --- | ---
L476: `0`  | `Default`  | 1-on-1 DMs, invitation to groups, etc  | 14 days
L477: `2`  | `UserProfile`  | User profile config (display name, avatar)  | 30 days
L478: `3`  | `UserContacts`  | Contacts list config  | 30 days
L479: `4`  | `ConvoInfoVolatile`  | Volatile conversation state (forced unread, last msg read)  | 30 days
L480: `5`  | `UserGroups`  | User's groups and communities config  | 30 days
L481: `11`  | `ClosedGroupMessages`  | Groups v2 messages  | 14 days
L482: `12`  | `ClosedGroupKeys`  | Groups v2 encryption keys config  | 30 days
L483: `13`  | `ClosedGroupInfo`  | Groups v2 group info config  | 30 days
L484: `14`  | `ClosedGroupMembers`  | Groups v2 member list config  | 30 days
L485: `-11`  | `ClosedGroupRevokedRetrievableMessages`  | Group config visible to revoked members  | 14 days
L486: Config namespaces get a longer TTL than message namespaces to make the app state more resilient. Those are also usually pruned, so not many messages are expected to be stored in them. For instance, a user should only have one `UserProfile` config, as each devices should delete the previous one when pushing a new one.
L487: ### Authentication per Namespace
L488: 
L489: Each namespace tier has a different authentication requirement on the store request:
L490: 
L491: Namespace(s)  | Auth required
L492: --- | ---
L493: `0` (Default)  | None - pubkey only
L494: `2, 3, 4, 5` (user config)  | signature with the user's own keypair
L495: `11` (group messages)  | subaccount signature (issued by group admin) or admin signature

Inspected and pinned upstream source for Signal Desktop, Session Desktop, Element Desktop/Seshat and Telegram Desktop.

- Signal and Session demonstrate SQLCipher with FTS5 for local desktop message search. Signal also explicitly configures WAL, full synchronization and commit-hook checkpointing.
- Element demonstrates a separately managed local event index with ingestion, deletion and schema recovery. Its optional dependency and passphrase fallback qualify any blanket claim about at-rest protection.
- Telegram’s inspected code establishes encrypted local domain/account records under `tdata`. It provides no evidence about the full transcript store or server-side engine.

These are source-level comparisons. They support retaining SQLCipher while measuring search and indexing alternatives, and provide no comparative latency or resource measurements. Exact revisions and source links were sent to the parent.
